payload.dispatch: Returning from a family holiday on 3 September 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that one of his culture plates was contaminated with a fungus, and that the colonies of staphylococci immediately around it had been destroyed. The laboratory where he made the discovery is preserved at St Mary's Hospital in London. Born in Ayrshire, Scotland, in 1881, Fleming shared the 1955 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of penicillin with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.

evidence.title: The prize
evidence.text: Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain 'for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases'.

evidence.title: The plate
evidence.text: On 3 September 1928, Fleming returned to his laboratory having spent a holiday with his family at Suffolk. The laboratory in which he discovered and tested penicillin is preserved as a museum in St Mary's Hospital, Paddington. He was born on 6 August 1881 near Darvel, in Ayrshire, Scotland.

reveal.explanation: The Nobel Prize came in 1945, ten years earlier than the dispatch said. The date of the discovery, the hospital and Fleming's birth year in 1881 are all correct.

sources.excerpt: On 3 September 1928, Fleming returned to his laboratory having spent a holiday with his family at Suffolk. On his return, Fleming noticed that one culture was contaminated with a fungus, and that the colonies of staphylococci immediately surrounding the fungus had been destroyed. The laboratory in which Fleming discovered and tested penicillin is preserved as the Alexander Fleming Laboratory Museum in St Mary's Hospital, Paddington. Born on 6 August 1881 at Lochfield farm near Darvel, in Ayrshire, Scotland. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.
